definition: Populism is political rhetoric that constructs a morally meaningful opposition between ordinary, virtuous people and a powerful, corrupt, self-serving, distant, or unresponsive elite, establishment, government, or special interest, often claiming that politics should restore control to the people or that the speaker authentically represents them.
inclusion_criteria: Code a text as populism when it contains a clear people-versus-elite or people-versus-establishment antagonism, especially when it does one or more of the following: (1) portrays ordinary citizens, workers, families, farmers, taxpayers, or voters as a unified and morally legitimate people; (2) identifies political, governmental, corporate, financial, professional, or other elites as corrupt, incompetent, self-serving, distant, or serving narrow interests; (3) presents government as controlled by or serving special interests rather than the public; (4) calls for the people to reclaim, control, or directly shape government; or (5) presents the speaker or a movement as the authentic vehicle of the people's will against established institutions. A mere reference to citizens, public opinion, social hardship, government failure, patriotism, policy disagreement, or partisan conflict is insufficient without this antagonistic and moralized people-versus-elite framing.
positive_example: "It's going to be a victory for the people. A victory for the everyday citizen whose voice hasn't been heard. It will be a win for the voters—not the pundits, not the journalists, not the lobbyists, not the global special interests funding my opponent's campaign." This explicitly presents ordinary voters as the legitimate people and opposes them to lobbyists, pundits, journalists, and global special interests. It therefore meets the inclusion criteria. Another positive example is: "The constant partisan rancor ... is what happens when people go to Washington to work for themselves and not you." This contrasts self-serving political insiders with ordinary citizens and presents the speaker as working for the latter.
negative_example: "The document discusses education, healthcare, economic capacity, and national strength. Although it briefly contrasts voters 'down here' with leaders 'up there,' it does not develop a clear people-versus-elite or anti-establishment populist framing." This is not populism because the brief spatial contrast is not developed into a moralized conflict. Similarly, a passage that merely advocates social programs, criticizes an opposing party's platform, discusses military strength, or expresses faith in the people without identifying a corrupt or self-serving opponent should be coded as non-populist.
edge_case_rules: No classification record had confidence below 50, so there is no separately identified less-than-50-confidence category. For borderline cases, apply the inclusion criteria strictly: references to 'the people,' voters, workers, families, or local communities alone do not establish populism; neither do generic accusations of incompetence, corruption, policy failure, or partisan disagreement. Code as populism when the text links such accusations to a broader claim that an elite, establishment, government, or special interest is illegitimately opposed to or betraying ordinary people, or when it explicitly calls for restoring government to popular control. Foreign tyrants or geopolitical adversaries count only when the passage frames them as oppressors of a people and liberation as the rightful popular cause. A direct anti-government appeal may qualify even without the word 'elite' when government is portrayed as ruling over, exploiting, or displacing the people. If the antagonism is merely implied and the passage is otherwise conventional campaign rhetoric, code it as non-populist.
edge_case_example: "So, you've got to think of that. ... The way to progress is not through programs which, in effect, will say, 'Turn over all these problems to the Federal Government. Let us have your money and we'll spend it for you.' The way to progress is for the Federal Government to do what it ought to do ... but not to spend a dollar that can be spent better by the people themselves at home right here in Marietta, Ohio." Although this does not explicitly name a corrupt elite, it treats local ordinary people as more capable and legitimate than distant federal government and opposes centralized authority to popular self-government. Under the edge-case rule for implicit people-versus-government framing, it should be coded as populism. Another borderline example is: "The passage invokes popular crowds and a forceful anti-incumbent battle cry calling for the existing political leadership to be thrown out." The crowd's call to remove established leadership is sufficient anti-establishment framing when understood as a popular challenge to the political order.
